articles.title: Handling Poison Messages in AWS Event-Driven Pipelines
articles.excerpt: Imagine a hypothetical production pipeline where a Lambda function consumes events from an Amazon SQS queue to perform schema validation and write records to an Amazon DynamoDB table. One afternoon, a…
articles.body: Imagine a hypothetical production pipeline where a Lambda function consumes events from an Amazon SQS queue to perform schema validation and write records to an Amazon DynamoDB table. One afternoon, an upstream system pushes a malformed JSON payload that misses a required primary key. The Lambda function crashes, SQS puts the message back in the queue after the visibility timeout expires, and the function immediately consumes the same bad message again. This "poison message" loop creates a self-inflicted denial-of-service attack, inflating your execution costs and delaying the processing of valid downstream events. In event-driven architectures, poison messages are inevitable.
articles.author: Aniket Abhishek Soni

articles.title: 1/7 is a whole number. Your number system just hasn't heard yet.
articles.excerpt: People invented numbers, and the rules you learned in school are one choice. Change a single rule and you get a different number system, just as solid, that mathematicians have used for over a century…
articles.body: People invented numbers, and the rules you learned in school are one choice. Change a single rule and you get a different number system, just as solid, that mathematicians have used for over a century. In that one, 1 ÷ 7 is a whole number. Grab a calculator. This takes two minutes, and you'll see it happen. 1. Square 5. Then keep going. 5 × 5 = 25 25 × 25 = 625 625 × 625 = 390625 390625 × 390625 = 152587890625 Look at the end of each answer. It stops changing. …625 shows up and never leaves, then …90625 , then …890625 . Each step locks in at least one more digit on the right, sometimes several at once. Keep squaring forever and the ending freezes into one endless number that runs off to the left : …918212890625 and here's the weird part: that number is its own square.

articles.body: Last week a reader pushed back on something I wrote about proving which model answered a request. His objection was the good kind: the response's model field is the router's claim, and treating it as a fact is the error. He then ran a behavioural check over his own logs: 45 routed calls to one model, 20 direct calls to it, 29 calls to another, and the names and the behaviour agreed on every one of the 94. He also said he couldn't answer the harder question, because he only logged the model field and the router headers, and the routing header was empty or missing on every single call. So I went and read one router's documentation instead of arguing. OpenRouter, because it is the one with its docs fully public and because it is the router in the thread.

articles.title: Humidifier Sizing in Python: Track Humidity Ratio, Not RH
articles.excerpt: Relative humidity is the number everyone reads and the wrong one to compute with. Heat 15°F air at 70% RH to 70°F and it drops to about 8% RH, yet not a single grain of water was added or removed. If…
articles.body: Relative humidity is the number everyone reads and the wrong one to compute with. Heat 15°F air at 70% RH to 70°F and it drops to about 8% RH, yet not a single grain of water was added or removed. If your code stores humidity as RH and carries it through a heating step, every downstream number is wrong. The variable that survives heating and cooling is the humidity ratio W: pounds of water per pound of dry air (or grains per pound, 7,000 grains = 1 lb). This post builds a small humidifier-sizing model around W, using the psychrometric equations from the ASHRAE Handbook of Fundamentals, and ends with a result that runs against intuition: on the coldest days a house needs less humidifier water, not more.

articles.title: Your 27-model ensemble has 1.5 opinions: measuring diversity with Fleiss' kappa and lineage-weighted voting
articles.excerpt: An ensemble is a claim about independence. You put k models in a room, they vote, and errors unique to each member cancel out. That only works if members actually disagree. If they all came from the s…
articles.body: An ensemble is a claim about independence. You put k models in a room, they vote, and errors unique to each member cancel out. That only works if members actually disagree. If they all came from the same handful of prompts, voting is theatre. Our platform has 3,784 model records and 46,807 graded calls over 16,787 fixtures. On paper that is a deep committee. I measured how deep with three estimators: stance concentration, pairwise contradiction, and Fleiss' kappa converted to effective ensemble size. On the 2,722 fixtures with five or more voters, the average ballot held 10.34 models and 1.46 effective opinions . A majority vote over those ballots scored 56.95% — slightly worse than the 57.00% average of the members it aggregated.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

articles.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
articles.excerpt: SpaceX just made spaceflight history, catching the upper stage of its Starship megarocket when it returned to Earth. But Starship still has some pretty big boxes left to check.
articles.body: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off. Long-distance view of Ship's historic landing on Nov. 14, 2026.
